chunks: Ḥammād ibn ʿUthmān narrated from al-Ḥalabī, from Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, who said:
I asked him about a man who said to his wife, “You are separate from me,” or “absolved,” or “final,” or “separated,” or “forbidden.” He said: “It is nothing.”

key_terms.بَائِنٌ: a term indicating separation or irrevocability
key_terms.بَتَّةٌ: a term suggesting finality or severance
key_terms.بَرِيئَةٌ: a phrase indicating disavowal or absolution
key_terms.حَرَامٌ: a phrase declaring the wife forbidden
key_terms.خَلِيَّةٌ: a formula implying release or separation from the marital bond
key_terms.لَيْسَ بِشَيْءٍ: it has no legal effect; it does not count

ai.seo_question: Do phrases like ‘you are separate from me’ or ‘you are forbidden to me’ count as divorce in Islamic law?
ai.summary: This hadith gives a legal ruling concerning divorce expressions. Imam Abū ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام states that these phrases, by themselves, do not constitute a valid divorce and have no legal effect.

en.bab-ul-qaim-publications: Hadith.4889 - Hammad ibn Uthman narrated from Al-Halabi who narrated from Abu Abdullah (as) that

Imam (as) was asked about a man who said to his wife, "You are free from me," or "You are absolved," or "You are finalized," or "You are separated," or "You are forbidden."
Imam (as) replied: "It amounts to nothing."
